speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER OF AUSTRALIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my privilege today to call the attention of the house to the presence in the Speaker's gallery of Right Hon. John McEwen, deputy prime minister of the commonwealth of Australia. Mr. McEwen has been a most distinguished leader not only in his own country but throughout the commonwealth of nations, and in 1958 he headed the Australian delegation to the trade and economic conference in Montreal. He comes to us following a stay in Washington. He is discussing with members of the government matters of international interest, including in particular the implications of the common market, as the entry of the United Kingdom may affect not only our two nations but commonwealth trade relations as a whole. To him, and through him, I extend warmest good wishes.
We recall so well an address which was given in the days of war by the prime minister of Australia, Right Hon. Robert Menzies. It will always be remembered by those who were privileged to hear it. Speaking in this chamber with great eloquence, he filled us with determination and moved us to a realization of those values which were then at stake.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER OF AUSTRALIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to join with the Prime Minister in welcoming to our country Right Hon. Mr. McEwen, the deputy prime minister of Australia. Our relationship with this commonwealth country has been not only cordial but very close at the United Nations and all international meetings. I am sure that those of us who sit on this side of the house will not only be happy to welcome the deputy prime minister here but will also desire to wish him well in the deliberations that I am sure he will be entering upon with the government.

With the consent of the house, Mr. Speaker, I should like to add only this. Since the talks to be held will also have reference to the

common market and, consequently, to the export trade which is of particular concern to all of us, we hope that they will be successful.
On behalf of members of the opposition, I extend our best wishes to the deputy prime minister of Australia.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, members of this group join with the Prime Minister and the hon. member for Laurier in extending a welcome to the deputy prime minister of Australia. We in this group have a high appreciation of the value of the commonwealth and the role it can play in international affairs. On that account we are particularly anxious on all occasions to extend a most hearty welcome to any representatives of the people from our fellow commonwealth countries.
I was interested to hear the reference made by the Prime Minister to the study of the question of the common market. I am sure this is a matter of mutual and serious concern to Canada and Australia. I trust that after the discussions which will take place in the next few days we will reach a common approach to this question as fellow members of the commonwealth who are concerned with developments in this respect.

speechtext: If the house will give me leave I shall be glad to make a brief statement about experiments in reporting our proceedings by mechanical means, pursuant to the authority given by the house last April. My reason for suggesting what might be called a progress report is to remove doubts which may have been left in the minds of hon. members yesterday when the matter was raised, but not proceeded with, as a question of privilege. Is it agreed that I may make a brief statement?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: If hon. members will refer to page 3963 of Hansard of April 25, 1961 or the Journals of that year at page 471, they will see the following:

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
By leave of the house-and I should first inform the house that I have already consulted the party leaders-I should like to ask for the approval of the house to carry out some experiments in reporting the proceedings of the house by using tape recording machines in conjunction with our sound amplification system. The purpose is to determine whether mechanical recording can usefully be used in combination with

House of Commons
shorthand reporting, as is being done in some other jurisdictions, and to develop this information for the guidance of the committee on procedure and of the house itself. As I have said, nothing is contemplated other than experimental recordings. Is it agreed?	,___ ...

Agreed.
Before the July adjournment some experiments with dictaphone machines were made in the English and French debates offices with the co-operation of the editors and certain members of the staff. These experiments were not reported last session to the committee on procedure because they were not considered conclusive and the committee itself had its hands full with other business.
To continue the experiments the assistance of the management analysis division of the civil service commission was requested. This request was initiated by the Clerk on October 5, 1961, and the terms of reference were as follows:
To survey the organization, methods and procedures of the English debates reporting branch with a view to making recommendations for their improvement.
Mr. A. M. Ervin was assigned to the work. He has undertaken a fairly broad study of reporting methods elsewhere as well as in our own house.
The recordings which are now going on began on Thursday, March 1 and continued to March 9. The second stage will begin on March 15 and will run until March 23 and conclude at that point. The method is to take ten minute sample recordings at intervals of approximately one hour during the daily sessions.
In all these experiments the belts or discs on which the proceedings are recorded have been closely guarded and put to no outside, ulterior or improper use. The belts and tapes from the first experiment have been destroyed, and those from Mr. Ervin's experiments will be turned over to the Speaker with his report. There has been nothing secret about the experiments other than to maintain the privacy of the records.
I think perhaps hon. members would like me to add that what we are doing should not be taken in any way as a reflection on our excellent reporting and editorial staff, but rather as an attempt at finding possible means of assisting them in their difficult duties.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to address a question to the Prime Minister. I trust he realizes that these questions are advanced in a spirit of cooperation to assist him to unveil this mystery and deal effectively with future situations.
In view of the report in the Globe and Mail of March 15 that soldiers caught smuggling in Indo-China late in 1961 were dealt with on the spot by their commanding officers, and apparently quite lightly; and since under the National Defence Act the maximum punishment that can be imposed by a commanding officer is three months' detention, could the Prime Minister inform the house why so lenient a view was taken of these deplorable crimes, and could he assure the house that all future proven cases of smuggling by members of the armed forces will be dealt with by courtmartial?

Mr. Speaker, I think this question should more properly have been addressed to me as Minister of National Defence. First of

Inquiries of the Ministry all I should like to say that I think the hon. member has a rather peculiar view of the administration of justice, in that the whole tenor of his question was along the line that any person suspected or accused of a particular crime is more or less automatically guilty and must be dealt with accordingly. When a man in the army is suspected of a particular crime-and the same thing applies in civil life-the first thing that has to be done is to secure sufficient evidence to establish a prima facie case. On the basis of what the investigation discloses the man's commanding officer determines whether he should be dealt with summarily or whether he should be tried by courtmartial. It is not the function of the government to state that a particular case shall be dealt with by court-martial. Is is for the law officers in the J.A.G.'s branch, the commanding officer and the commander of the command that the man happens to be in to determine the particular procedure to be followed. I can assure the hon. member and other hon. members that all due regard is being paid to the proper course that should be followed in the administration of justice in the army.

I wonder whether the hon. member, before he begins, would permit me to make certain observations concerning the supplementary estimates, which have now been before the committee of supply for some days. The further supplementary estimates No. 3, which are those we are now concerned with, were introduced some time ago and have already engaged the attention of the committee of supply on, I believe, six days, today being the seventh. There are altogether 61 items before us, only 22 of which have been discussed and passed thus far.
My colleague the Minister of Veterans Affairs, leading the house, drew to the attention of the house on two occasions the serious consequences that were certain to result from delay in dealing with these important supplementary estimates. On March 8, as reported at page 1635 of Hansard, my colleague said:
I had hoped that we would finish the supplementary estimates this week because we are spending more than the normal time on supplementaries, and there will still be final supplementaries coming before us during this month. But uncertain as to whether or not we will complete the supplementaries tomorrow, I cannot forecast the business for Monday and Tuesday.
If we do not finish the supplementaries we might have to continue with them on Monday, because certain works will come to an end and people will be without pay unless we are able to get these supplementaries approved.
Again on March 12, as reported at page 1731 of Hansard, my colleague drew to the attention of the house the serious consequences of delay. He said on that occasion:
-as I pointed out to the house last week, certain projects will have to be discontinued for lack of money to carry them on and certain people will go without their pay because the money has not been voted by parliament.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, all of them; and an opportunity of discussing the other estimates that are before us now.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I recognize the hon. member for Timiskaming.
26207-1-1161
Supply-Labour

This has been a very interesting discussion, but in my opinion it has not been very fruitful. On behalf of this party I should like to add only one suggestion, namely that I hope it is not a prelude to the government using governor general's warrants.
I rise on a question of privilege.
Sit down.
Before the hon. member continues, will he allow me to observe that the Minister of Finance who raised this matter has now left the chamber while this matter is still under discussion.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: A disgraceful statement.
He is back.
They have brought him back.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member for Essex East has just made a statement-
I raised a question of privilege.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -which he put forward obviously with a view to drawing attention to the fact that I had departed from the chamber when the hon. member for Timiskaming began to speak on the next item. I had expected to leave the chamber. I am leaving for a very good reason, namely to attend a very important meeting with the deputy prime minister of Australia, for which meeting I am now 10 minutes late. That is the reason I left the chamber. It was not that there was anything uninteresting about the remarks of the hon. member for Timiskaming, and it certainly was not for the reasons assigned by the hon. member for Essex East.
I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman.
Contempt of parliament by the Minister of Finance.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must remind the committee that the hon. member for Timiskaming has the floor, and that I had recognized him.

You apparently did not hear me, Mr. Chairman, because of the noise opposite. I was raising a point of order, and it is this. Your Honour tolerated a lecture by the Minister of Finance to this committee. In the course of that lecture he made reflections about the conduct of other hon. members of the committee, and raised certain

Supply-Labour
points. He even threatened us with responsibility for the failure to pay public servants, and so on.
Where is the point of order?
Surely, Mr. Chairman, I will be permitted to explain my point of order.

Take 20 minutes.
Another hon. Member: What is the point of order?
Mr. Chairman, may I ask you to keep order?
Oh, oh.

When in the committee it was agreed that something be raised that is irrelevant, it has been the custom that the debate should not be choked off as long as hon. members wished to debate the matter. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River rose in order to put to the Minister of Finance a very pertinent question, but he was not recognized. This debate initiated by the Minister of Finance has been terminated while hon. members still wished to discuss points which he raised. I suggest that this is a denial of the rights of the opposition that is intolerable.
Oh, oh.

We are surely entitled to know which estimates were made so badly last year that the minister is now running out of money, and to have disclosed the real amount of mismanagement that made it necessary for a threat to be made on the orders of the day.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The Minister of Finance asked permission to make a general remark, which he made, and it was made by the leave of the committee. That remark was made and an adequate reply was given by the opposition. We are not here studying the rules of procedure of the House of Commons. The business before the committee is vote No. 636. I would ask all hon. members to co-operate with the Chair so that we may get down to the business that is now before the committee, namely vote No. 636. On that particular business, which is the only business the Chair can deal with at all, I have recognized the hon. member for Timiskaming.

Mr. Chairman, as a P.S. to this whole debate I would advise our civil servants to get down to the banks and cash their cheques just in case. Yesterday we were talking about the fact that in Ontario we seem to have gone into the construction of these vocational schools without arriving at
[Mr. Pickersgill.)
firm plans as to how we are going to get the children into them, what the purpose of the training will be, and also what the end result will be with respect to the students going through these schools.
I was pointing out to the hon. member for York-Scarborough in particular-when he speaks again in this debate I should like to know whether he does not believe this is true-that it is my information that in his area it is the expectation that during the next four or five years many of the classrooms being built under this program will be high school classrooms because there will not be the vocational teachers or vocational students to put into those particular classrooms.
Have you no faith in Canada?

Certainly we have faith in Canada, but we have very little faith that le bon Dieu or somebody else is going to decide this matter. We should do a little planning. We should make some preparations. In Ontario the minister of education who is going to be responsible for this program is also the premier. A person who listened to the debate yesterday from the gallery asked me last night if I had heard about Robart's program of robots in the classrooms. Maybe we are going to use robots for teaching purposes. Maybe this is the way it should be done, but I do not think this kind of program can be undertaken without a plan. We know that we have not the facilities in Ontario to train teachers; we have not the facilities to train guidance councillors, yet the vocational training program in Ontario is more than double what it formerly was.
Does the hon. member want an answer to his question right now?
What about the hon. member for Peterborough?

I am sure the hon. member will understand the difference between academic training and technical training. Some other members may not. They may not know it is very difficult to transform the one into the other and get the best results. I am sure the minister will be the first to accept my statement that the plan has grown out of all proportion, and that it was certainly not expected that it would be so widely accepted; but because it has been widely accepted additional assistance will have to be provided to make the plan successful.
The third field into which I think the federal government should go immediately has to do with the establishment of standards for career and guidance teachers and other counsellors. Some members can laugh about this if they want to, but it is going to be of vital importance. The parents of children entering technical, vocational or business schools today are vitally concerned about whether they have chosen the right occupation for their children. I can only speak for the province of Ontario where I think the situation has been made more difficult because the whole system is now being broken into three sections and students who now do not have to choose a career until they have graduated from high school are going to have to make a decision at a much earlier age.
Mr. Pallet!: Would the hon. member permit a question? Has he not read the proposed program in detail?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Or the act?
I do not quite understand the hon. member.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Has he not read either the act under which these estimates are required or the program that has been announced by the minister of education for Ontario? If he has, then his last statement cannot possibly stand up.
Supply-Labour

The parliamentary secretary should know that we are not discussing a bill but rather a supplementary estimate. He should also know that the province of Ontario has not finally determined its program. If they have, it has not been made known to northern Ontario. A parent-teacher meeting was held in one of the new vocational schools about a week ago and nobody was prepared to give any of the answers or I would not be raising the problem. I believe these things have not been settled. If the hon. member has knowledge that I do not have, then I would appreciate knowing where the teachers are going to come from.
That is not our concern.
That is the whole point. You say it is not your concern, but it has got to be your concern. There is no point in buying a car and having no gasoline for it.
You are out of order.

There we have this government all over again. We say that you do not really care, but you have to care or the plan will be unsuccessful, and you will be dealing with the lives of a whole generation of children in the process. Vocational training is vitally needed. It has been needed for 50 years. Maybe it was needed then more than now. I am not in a position to say because I am not in the counselling field. I do know that we just have not got the people available to staff these schools, and I say that the government should take the lead in assisting the provincial governments in this regard. There are people much better qualified than I who will be speaking on this matter, and you can question them.
The point is that we need further assistance. The minister is certainly to be congratulated for having initiated this plan. The fact is that it has met with greater acceptance than he expected would be the case. It is also important that we give leadership in the provision of qualified personnel to staff these schools. Maybe we will be able to use television for teaching. Maybe we could supply robot assistance. Maybe there are other forms of teaching we could supply that would fulfil the need. I think it is true that this year we are not going to have enough teachers for all the classrooms and shops in the schools that are being completed. I only ask that more consideration be given, not that there be any curtailment of the plan. We now know there are very great weaknesses in the field of education.
I believe that in the field of vocational and technical training the federal government has a responsibility. We want to see standards established for employment purposes from

Supply-Labour
coast to coast. We want to see standards established for teaching proficiency from coast to coast. We want to see every assistance given, every modernization made, wherever it is possible. These things should be provided by the government to those provinces who want to take advantage of them.

In view of the questions of the hon. member for Timiskaming which were directed to me, I should like to reply. I should like also to express some disappointment that he did not offer me the bet which he started to offer me when he was cut off the other evening.
Who is taking up the time now? Listen to what the Minister of Finance said to me.
The hon. member for Essex East is lecturing the committee.
I am not objecting, but just listen to what the Minister of Finance said. That is what I am pointing out.
As I was saying, before we were treated to another spontaneous lecture by the hon. member for Essex East-
Never mind the insults.
Still out of order; still speaking from your seat.
Why don't you try to speak from your head?

The hon. member for Timiskaming suggested there would not be a sufficient number of students in the township of Scarborough to fill the classrooms that are now being built under this program. I just want to say that I have more faith in the potential birth rate of York-Scarbor-ough than he has.
I did not say there would not be enough students. I said that there would not be enough in the technical courses. There will be enough students.
I am replying to precisely that point. There has been a substantial and continuing increase, a natural rate of increase in my constituency, possibly the highest rate of increase in Canada.
Does the hon. member have any control over that?
Quit bragging.

There is an increase in the number of young people with young families moving into this constituency. There have been over 100,000 move into the area since

the 1957 election. I suggest to the hon. member that he is insulting the intelligence and smearing the integrity of the officials of the department of education who were responsible for making these recommendations. The criticism by the hon. member for Timiskaming amounts to this. He is saying, in effect, that this government is moving too fast, moving too aggressively, and that is an interesting contrast to the statements made by members of both his party and particular sections of the frontbenchers who usually speak from their seats. They say that we have done too little and are too late in our efforts to combat this continuing, long term problem in this country.

When we opened the discussion of supplementary estimates No. 3 this afternoon I endeavoured to take the first opportunity to reply to the observations that had been advanced by the Minister of Finance. We are now dealing with a very substantial item in respect of vocational training. The Chair recognized the Minister of Finance, who intervened to suggest that there were people in Canada who were going to be deprived of salaries, under this item and other items in the supplementary estimates, because parliament was not dealing expeditiously with these proposed expenditures. It was not possible for me to be recognized, although I attempted to obtain the recognition of the Chair while the Minister of Finance was in his seat. I feel that if I had been able to obtain recognition the hon. member for Timiskaming would have recogized that I was speaking to the point that was then under discussion, and he would have allowed me to continue.
I want to say that the responsibility in these matters is with the government and is always with the government. These supplementary estimates No. 3 were introduced on February 8, 1962 by the Minister of Finance. However, not until February 23 was this committee asked to deal with them. Then again, there was an adjournment of the debate on these matters. This is all within the leadership of the government. We were not again asked to deal with these matters until March 2 or 3, I believe.
In addition to that, and what I really rose to try to get information about, is the fact that the main estimates presented a year ago always contain what I call a kitty, something available to the Minister of Finance to prevent any failure in the payment of pressing obligations, particularly payments for personal services in the way of salaries. The main estimates for 1961-62 contain an item called "Contingencies and miscellaneous." Our government financial housekeepers should have

been looking ahead rather than coming now and moaning that perhaps somebody is not going to get a pay cheque.
This is the third group of supplementary estimates for the current fiscal year. Further supplementary estimates No. 2 were introduced on January 24. Was there anything in them to replenish the so-called kitty to which I referred, and which is given to the Minister of Finance every year in his main estimates? Was there anything advanced by him after parliament assembled, in the further supplementary estimates No. 2, for the replenishing of another kitty, item No. 125, to supplement other votes subject to the approval of treasury board, for the payment of salaries, wages and other pay list expenses? There was not. There is nothing of that nature advanced in supplementary estimates No. 3.
I want to say that had there been, this would have been taken care of, because items for the Minister of Finance were given priority. I remind the committee that the supplementary estimates for the Minister of Finance were passed at the first opportunity for debate, on February 23. There was no item to replenish these votes. I should like, therefore, to ask the parliamentary secretary to tell me to what extent his opportunity to take care of the situation by means of these items has been completely lost. I refer to the votes that we passed, items 121 and 125 in the main estimates. I say it is completely erroneous to tell those who are looking to the government for payment for personal services, or for materials, that the opposition is to blame if they are not paid.
I repeat that the supplementary estimates were presented on February 8. The leader of the house did not introduce them for debate until February 23. We were given then only one day of debate and the next opportunity for debate, I think, was March 12. I say that no blame can accrue to the opposition in this respect.
I do want the Minister of Finance to indicate, without any derogation of our rights as an opposition-after all, there is a lot of money involved here-which of the items we have not yet passed involve payment for personal services which the minister is not already empowered to deal with under the general "kitty" items to which I have referred.

Mr. Chairman, it is with no apology that I take up the time of this committee to deal with this problem, because I do not think there is any piece of legislation, and certainly no estimate, which will
Supply-Labour
have more effect and significance in the years ahead than the one we are dealing with this afternoon.
Hon. members know that this program comes under Bill No. C-49, which was introduced in the fall of last year. We all had great hopes for this program and we all supported the bill with a considerable amount of enthusiasm, although not without some serious misgivings. I am afraid those misgivings have proven to be justified.
If I may trace the history of this matter for a moment, this was a crash program, but it was a crash program in an area where crash programs are least successful, and I am afraid that the whole thing may come crashing down around us. We all know the pressure that was behind this program. In the fall of 1960 the unemployment crisis had reached tremendous heights and something had to be done. This was one of those great pieces of legislation put forward to solve and end our unemployment problem.
However, a second realization came along with it. This was as a result of studies that were made in certain areas in certain occupations, when we discovered that Canada had one of the worst trained work forces in the world. Indeed, over the last 10 or 15 years we had been importing our skilled labour and had failed rather miserably to create a society which would encourage young people to stay at school and become more skilled and more able to compete in the technical and vocational areas when their lack of skill was the cause of their being unemployed.
We brought those two facts together and then, of course, we made a rather amazing assumption. We assumed that the provision of facilities, the building of schools, shops, and so on would solve this problem. We assumed this was the deficiency with which we had to deal, that we had not built enough vocational schools at the secondary level, not enough trade schools at the post-secondary level, and certainly not enough technical institutions for a higher level of attainment. This was a reasonable assumption, but I do not think it is one that has ever been borne out by the facts.
Last May the information branch of Department of Labour passed around a publication which I am sure all hon. members have received. It contains a series of speeches on education, training and employment. It was published and distributed by the information branch of the Department of Labour in May, 1961. In this publication there is an address by Mr. D. E. Bridge, of the vocational training branch of the Department of Labour, which

Supply-Labour
deals with this problem of facilities. I should like to quote the following extract:
In Canada at the present time there are 24 institutions of technology providing post-high school technical training and five institutes that offer both post-high school technical and also trade courses. In addition to these schools, approximately 223 technical, vocational or composite high schools provide commercial, technical, trade or other occupational training programs.
A cursory glance at these statistics will show where the real deficiency was; not in the secondary school level but in the postsecondary trade school level. In the trade school level there were five institutions across the whole Dominion of Canada. This is the area where the 700,000 people who were unemployed last winter could have obtained some relief. These were the people who did not have necessary skills; these were the people who were working in areas where they required new skills, and schools of this type in which they would be able to bring up their qualifications. This was an area where I think even a cursory glance would show what facilities were required. Mr. Bridge goes on to say:
At the post-high school technical training level, where requirements are developing rapidly, the shortage of training facilities is very acute.
I repeat, "very acute". He goes on to say:
There is a need for facilities for an additional
15.000	persons in full time day classes at the trade occupational and post-high school technical level.
Of course we recognized that need. At no point does Mr. Bridge say that at the secondary school level there is any very acute shortage. The reason for my interest in this matter is because in my own experience I have travelled around various schools where there was no great shortage in the technical classes and sections of the schools or where students were unable to take vocational courses because of such a shortage. In many areas where I went I found they had vacancies. I am talking now about the secondary school level.
Let us look at Ontario for a moment. The problem of facilities I contend, is not at the secondary school level. The minister's report of September, 1960 stated that there were 61,049 people in vocational training-this, of course, includes commercial and various types of vocational training-at the secondary school level. I made inquiries and found that the total facilities in the province of Ontario were capable of accepting approximately
70.000	people. In other words there were sufficient facilities, as far as I could determine, at the secondary school level.
How fast is the need growing? I took the figures for the last three years and found that the need had grown by about one tenth each year. The buildings which have already been

contructed, to say nothing of those contemplated by March, 1963, would raise the accommodation nearly 100 per cent from what it was when this bill was brought in. Once again I am talking about the secondary school level. Obviously one cannot help wondering whether these governments, especially the Ontario government, are not linking the development of secondary school training with reality. If they can get 75 cents for every dollar spent on this type of building, there is no reason why they should not take it. Whether they actually need it now or not.
There is no system of priority. We suggested when this bill was brought in that there should be a system of priority as to where the need was. Obviously it was in the post-secondary schools and in the trade schools. But where has all the money gone? We will look at the statistics on that question in just a moment.
Really What we have here is some kind of sewer view of education that was linked very closely to the N.H.A. legislation. It was suggested that we should build sewers and this would help put people to work, and it was felt that therefore if we built schools it would put people to work. The time limit was set for March, 1963 so we could build schools and other facilities whether or not we knew what we were doing. I suggest that one cannot relate the building of schools to a make work project; yet, as the minister said in reply to the hon. member for Timmins recently, the cut-off date of March 31 related to winter works. It is astounding to me that the long range future and employment of young people is being determined by winter works projects considerations. I think this will go down in the annals of education as one of the most fantastic, most misdirected programs ever conceived on the North American continent.
I read the debate on this bill with some amazement. At no time was it made clear exactly what the shortage was and where it was. I realize that the emphasis on keeping young people at school and the need for educational training in schools is important, and that with the growth of the population in this country we need more technical schools, but I say this is one of the most unbelievable hoaxes that has ever been perpetrated. This government does not know where the money is going or where it is coming from. This government has gone off on a wild spending spree which is unrelated entirely to where the real shortage is.
Mr. Bridge also says:
Early last fall the Department of Labour was requested to gather information on a national basis concerning the requirements for training in all areas. Its officials were asked what facilities were available then, what new accommodation was

required, what equipment and personnel were required to put the expanded program into operation.
I should like to read from the debate that took place on this program. Some rather interesting questions were asked in this connection. I can remember very well the afternoon when the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate came into the house and asked some rather interesting questions. I should like to read from page 675 of Hansard for December 9, 1960.

I am sure some survey of this was made before the legislation was produced and I would like the minister to tell us just what the capacity is in each province, how many people could be trained in the existing institutions that have already been provided and in each province, as well, what the department's estimate is of the deficiency. I ask that because I assume the department has made some kind of estimate of how many places for additional pupils are really required in order to do the much larger job which I completely agree with the minister needs to be done.
Then on page 676 appears the minister's answer:
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate asked about the present situation in vocational training schools in this country. I might say that I have had conferences, particularly with the province of Ontario, to see whether more of this training could be undertaken.
Boy, just look at the amount of money which is going to the province of Ontario now. The federal share amounts to more than $120 million. Quebec is getting $5 million and New Brunswick $1.8 million.
Have you the figure for British Columbia?
Yes, I have. It is $8 million. In Ontario it is $124 million.
Are those actual expenditures?
This is the table the minister gave-
Expenditures to date?
This is the estimated capital expenditure approved up to February 23, 1962.
Those are commitments.

That is right. Throughout history Ontario has been complaining about its money being used to help all the other provinces. All the provinces are educating Ontario now. "Particularly with the province of Ontario", the minister said. No wonder he should say that, when $125 million is being paid out of the money of this nation to Ontario and $5 million is going to the province of Quebec. To continue the quotation:
Their problem has been that all of their facilities have been filled to capacity.
Supply-Labour
I doubt that.
We have surveyed the other provinces of Canada-
I wonder why Ontario was picked out, especially when Premier Robarts came out and based practically all his campaign on a three stream system of education. But to continue-
We have surveyed the other provinces of Canada and we find their facilities are all filled to capacity and there is a waiting list.
I would question that also at the secondary level.
Almost as soon as the doors erf new accommodation are opened it is immediately filled. Consequently we feel with respect to this matter and as a result of our survey that there has to be at least a 50 per cent increase in capacity throughout the country so far as this type of school is concerned.
Then the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate continued:
What I am really trying to find out is how many individuals can be engaged in training with the present facilities on any one day? It is hard for me to believe that the government, which has reached the conclusion that the capacity should be increased 50 per cent, does not know what the capacity is right now.
Then comes the answer of the minister:
In this respect I am advised that all we can do is to take the word of the provinces. They are the ones who advise us in respect of these matters and it is the provinces who say that they feel that a 50 per cent increase in present capacity is necessary over the coming years.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate continued:
Is the minister really telling us that his department does not know what the present capacity is in this country? When all is said and done-
Then he was interrupted by the minister, who said:
I do not want any misunderstanding; that is exactly what I told you.
Isn't this unbelievable? I will go on to another remark of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate:
I say I would not, as a minister of the crown, come into this parliament and ask that public money be spent out of the treasury of Canada merely because a provincial government said they would like more of something, unless they told me precisely what they had already so that when I asked the representatives of the people who are the trustees of the people for their money, for more money, I could tell them what existed already and not merely say, we have to take the word of the provinces.
Well, apparently that Is the situation, and I cannot help wonder what this means. Somebody suggested that Premier Frost died
politically of heartbreak because the promises made by the Prime Minister in Massey hall were not kept. I think he died politically of hysterics at the thought that he could take

Supply-Labour
this government for everything it is worth. I think he must believe that they are the biggest group of suckers who ever landed here in Ottawa, because they can find a way to make this government pay for their education costs.
What does Premier Robarts say? He says "Cut down your education costs". I am reading from the Toronto daily Star of February 15:
Premier John Robarts last night warned that municipalities must hold the line on education expenditures to keep municipal taxes at a reasonable level.
In other words he is saying "Boy, we have got something good. Now we will hold the line and we will stick the federal government for every cent we can." This expenditure has become a kind of transfer payment from the federal government to the department of education in Toronto. I think the department itself must go into hysterics every time they realize what this government is doing.
What the minister is saying in this debate is, we are concerned about unemployment and we have an idea that technical training can do some good. We are not sure that the government can do any good, but we can go on giving money out, not merely to the provinces, but to the municipalities, to see what will happen.
How is this money being spent? The minister says, as reported at page 1778 of Hansard, that it is to be spent as follows:
Included in these projects are the construction of one new institute of technology, 18 new trade schools, five new combined trade schools and institutes of technology and some 114 new vocational high schools.
Over and above these new schools, alterations and additions will be made to five institutes of technology, 16 trade schools, two combined trade schools and institutes, 56 vocational high schools and 31 minor alterations.
The money is going to the wrong places at the wrong times and for the wrong reasons. Obviously the provincial governments are going to accept this. Why would they not accept it?
Are you going to vote against it?

We shall vote it even if it bankrupts you. The history of the opposition in this parliament has been voting for little bits and drops in the bucket. That has been the entire activity going on in this part of the house. May I continue? I want to read a part of a speech by Mr. Bridge:
The provinces were asked to estimate their needs and to suggest their possible expenditures for the next ten years. After considerable study of the needs of the ten provinces and a concentrated look in the crystal ball-

Boy, that was some crystal ball.
-we came up with an estimated cost of some $190 million which I will admit startled us but apparently did not startle the cabinet. They decided to plan new legislation which would provide the type of training which we thought necessary for our own skilled manpower training program.
That was for the next ten years; $190 million. This was the result of the survey made by the Department of Labour. I point out that we are up to $269 million already. The hon. member for York-Scarborough said we were questioning the intelligence of the staff of the Minister of Labour. What does he say now?
That was not what I said.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: And the curriculum?
You cannot conduct an art class in a woodworking shop.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I think we wanted to know if the hon. member thought the federal government should establish the curriculum for the schools.

I am not suggesting that. Let me place on the record a comment made by Dr. Claude Bissell, former president of Carle-ton University, when addressing the opening session of the Canadian conference on education in Montreal:
Current demands for more vocational training in Canadian schools are about 20 years too late-
Perhaps one of the best known commentaries on the educational scene is J. Bascom St. John, who writes for the Toronto Globe *and Mail. I invite hon. members opposite to listen to what he says:
If anything is clear, even to Ontario politicians, it is that education is changing just as society is changing. This means that new approaches will have to be developed in school architecture to make possible the new trends in education. (That is why it is a national tragedy to spend $200 million, as Ontario is doing, on technical schools designed for educational programs that are already out of date.)
I suggest that in many cases this is a problem communities will face. They will have vocational training schools preparing people for employment opportunities that existed in the 1930's and 1940's. They will be
Supply

Labour
training people for jobs of a nature for which there is a declining demand. The tragedy is that communities will be stuck with buildings that are out of date even before they are built.
Let me take an example. Last year I examined the woodworking program. I doubt that there is any job area that is less likely to expand or to be creative of employment than woodworking as it breaks down into cabinet making, pattern making, and so on.
I do not know the experience of other hon. members, but my own experience this winter substantiates my belief. I have received a great many calls from unemployed carpenters this winter.
I am sorry to again use the Ontario school system as an example, but when you consider the money spent in the province in this field it is perhaps good to examine the record. In 1958 there were 111 graduates in all branches of woodwork. In 1959 the figure declined to 109 and in 1960 it dropped to 91. When I directed an inquiry to the department I was advised that 117 new wings or new buildings had been constructed in Ontario and there were 81 woodworking shops, approximately one for every student graduating in the craft. One director of education commented that we might as well establish a program under which we would give courses in fur trading, which would be just about as relevant to the situation. No time is spent in thinking, planning or in conducting research. We are just handing out money. There is no research project to determine the direction we should follow. I suggest we are erecting buildings which will be future monuments to our lack of foresight.
One cannot but wonder at the order in which things are being done.
I wish to read from the Toronto daily Star of February 28 an article entitled "Add $28 Million to Build Technical Schools-Ottawa". It reads in part as follows:
Coupled with the building program la a report, soon to be released, surveying training requirements of industry across Canada and making recommendations as to what skills are most In demand.
Has this report been tabled? I have taken this comment from a news release. It continues:
The two year study was undertaken by H. L. Shepherd, industrial relations supervisor of Canadian Westinghouse in Hamilton.
What a backward way to go about it. You put the buildings up and then have the survey. Of course the survey may reveal that the existing buildings do not meet the needs and that you cannot adapt the buildings to meet the needs revealed by the survey. A

Supply-Labour
few millions should have been spent in research to find out where we are going; then the buildings could have been constructed. I suppose, however, that would not be politically expedient. I suggest that by 1963 there will be large numbers of brick piles to which cabinet ministers can point as they wander across the nation. The politicians are playing politics with the careers of our young people, and I am sure none of us condone this.
Let me quote from a news release issued by the Department of Labour on February 14, a statement attributed to the minister:
Because of the recent increase in federal financial assistance to vocational training facilities there has been a great growth in the training capacity of schools in all provinces Mr. Starr said. He added that this will provide more pre-employment training and more capacity for training employed persons, with great advantage to the apprenticeship program.
This expansion of training facilities is only the first phase of our work, Mr. Starr told the committee, which is made up of leading representatives from industry, the labour movement, and provincial departments of labour.
Surely the first phase should have been research to determine the needs. Can a more backward approach be imagined? I continue:
The federal government is not satisfied just to see more schools being built, the minister stated. We are interested in the programs that will be provided in these schools and in industry. We want to see these new schools serve adequately the youth of our country, and industry.
In other words, you build the buildings, then find out what the needs are, and then set up the program. That is simply too ridiculous. What terrible consequences there will be as a result of this preposterous sequence. It may be discovered that we do not need some of the buildings, some may be located in the wrong places, some may be fitted for the wrong courses and of course, tragically, we will be stuck with them for 25 or 30 years. It is already too late, and the buildings will decide the programs.
The provisions of Bill No. C-49 offer assistance in the training of teachers, and I shall have more to say about that later. However, I cannot conceive of a more backward way of dealing with what I consider to be one of the most serious problems in the nation. Will the sequence here be that of putting up buildings, retraining teachers already trained, studying the needs and then deciding on the program? Again the sequence is backward. We are faced with the problem of bringing people up to the levels of skill and technical training demanded by the age in which we live. The Ontario department is faced with over 100 technical wings springing up everywhere. Where will they find the teachers?

As hon. members probably realize, vocational education divides into two distinct phases; the industrial arts, which is an important and significant area of teaching, as well as vocational training which is largely related to providing jobs. We recently received an interesting telegram from the chairman of the research council. This is what he says:
Technical program in Ontario has caused displacement and discomfort for long established and professionally sound area of industrial arts. Research shows one hundred men seriously affected. Department not cooperating well to allow these to re-qualify but they take anybody from the trades. Details to follow. Sincerely feel with many others that program has gone overboard and is outdated.
What you have at this time-
The Depuiy Chairman: I am sorry; I thought the hon. member had finished his sentence.

We have industrial arts
teachers who are doing important work in one area placed in another area where they themselves recognize they are not as qualified to teach trades training or vocational training as are those who have had several years trades experience, as it has been in the past. What you have are people less qualified in that sense when we need men more qualified in a certain way.

I listened to the hon. member for Peterborough with great interest. I think he has made a very thoughtful address and one which deserves serious study by this government. I will not attempt in any way to repeat the arguments he has put forward, as he has made the case very well.
Does the hon. member agree with him?

Supply-Labour
training in academic subjects only; 38 men taking academic subjects plus welding; 21 men taking blueprint reading plus academic subjects; 29 men taking tor the last day cabinet making plus academic subjects.
On January 26, 1962, the following letter was received by Mr. F. Roca, past president of the Italian community promotion centre, from the prime minister, the Hon. John P. Robarts:
"Dear Mr. Roca:
Your telegram dated January 14, 1962, expressed regret on behalf of the Italian community regarding the decision which was reached with respect to a proposed training program at the provincial institute of trades. The matter of offering practical training in the building trades has been studied carefully and the conclusion has been reached that under the laws as they stand at present the Ontario department of education is not in a position to offer basic training for skilled development in the designated trades. The course has, therefore, been revised to include academic work related to the trades. It is our opinion that this revised course will be of value to the people whom you represent.
Yours sincerely,
John P. Robarts,
Prime Minister of Ontario and Minister of Education."
Some unanswered questions: In analysing these events, the following considerations have come to our attention:
1.	Out of 180 applicants, 45 have spent four to ten years as tradesmen and had registered for the course to upgrade themselves. It is difficult for us to understand the basis on which unemployed tradesmen are denied this opportunity.
2.	While the main purpose of the course is to upgrade these people academically, it is important to remember that these men are accustomed to manual work and that it is most difficult to get them to accept an educational program which excludes any opportunity to develop manual skills.
3.	We have been diligently studying the apprenticeship act and regulations in order to learn what precise laws in Ontario would make it illegal for the department of education to offer training in basic skills in designated trades where there is no compulsory certification. If it is entirely permissible for anyone over 21 years of age to accept employment in any of the building trades, whether he has any training or not, why then is it illegal for the department of education to provide this much desired training?
4.	We have been surprised to learn after careful investigation that Ontario is the only Canadian province where the apprenticeship act makes it impossible for a person over 21 to get training in a designated trade.
Summation:
It is our firm conviction that in watering down the progressive and comprehensive program it embarked upon last November the government has taken a retrograde step. We therefore call upon the members of the legislature to urge the government to alter its decision and return to its original policy. Failure to do so will, in our view, lead inevitably to a situation where thousands of new Canadians, who could by retraining very greatly enrich their own lives and thereby increase their value to the province of Ontario, will instead become spiritually disheartened and during frequent periods of unemployment an economic burden to the community. To permit this to happen would, in our opinion, be a denial of the dignity and rights which are the basis of the Ontario human rights code.
We hope that in reviewing the facts given above you will bear in mind that our organization, in
[Ur. Hellyer.l
pressing for the full reinstatement of the original plan, is motivated by one desire, to enable these new Canadian citizens to increase their knowledge and develop their skills so that they may make their maximum contribution to the development and progress of the land of their adoption. Above all, we hope that you will do your very utmost to bring about a speedy change in existing laws which now stand as a barrier to the government's previously announced retraining program.
We are confident that the members of the legislative assembly will share the concern felt by the members of our association in a situation where the well-being and future usefulness of many thousands of new Canadians is vitally affected. For that reason we felt obligated to provide you with some background material which will enable you to make a proper assessment of the problem and effect an early solution. It is our earnest hope that you will find the occasion to deal with this matter within your own parliamentary group or in the course of your legislative deliberations. If you desire further information the undersigned will be very happy to confer with you.
Respectfully submitted,
Adelsi Bulfoni, President.
Although this memorandum is oriented to new Canadians, it applies equally to all Canadians. They have the same problems. It applies equally to unemployed adults no matter what their origin who happen now to find themselves without employment and who wish to take advantage of their idleness to improve their chances to contribute gainfully to the country they love. This is the problem. This is what we are trying to face and yet this problem is being evaded by the government by reason of the administration it is giving to this act.
I have said that in respect of young people of high school age there is some real question whether further expenditure in this area is in their own best interests or whether, on the other hand, an expansion of the apprenticeship scheme would not be of greater benefit to them. I can say from my experience in hiring men, Mr. Chairman, that I have found that those who are best qualified and best able to go to work and do their assigned tasks well, without on the job training, are those who have gone through the apprenticeship system and those least qualified and least able to perform the duties assigned to them are those who in many cases have graduated from the secondary school system as it is now constituted.
This raises a very real and vital question. We are being asked to provide to the province of Ontario alone over $100 million. To do what? That is the question. To subsidize the building of secondary school facilities which are not in some cases in the best interests of the pupils themselves? Is that the purpose for which funds are being voted? Is it the intention of parliament that the great problem of unemployed adults is to be overlooked and ignored and that the impression is to be created that something is being

done merely because a lot of money is being spent? Is this what we are being asked to believe?
There is a very real question, Mr. Chairman, as to the effectiveness of this plan to meet the purposes for which it was allegedly designed. This raises too, as I have said, by inference at least a question as to the competence of the authorities in some of the provinces, particularly in my own province of Ontario, to administer the plan wisely and make the maximum use of the funds for the purpose for which they were intended. Frankly, I have not too much faith in the Ontario administration.
Furthermore, it raises the larger question of the effectiveness of provincial jurisdiction in labour matters. The judicial committee of the privy council ascribed labour matters to the provinces under section 92 of the British North America Act relating to property and civil rights. One could ask, how can the federal government, which is responsible for maintaining full employment, which is responsible for maintaining economic growth in the country, fulfil this responsibility when it is frustrated by legislation such as that existing in the province of Ontario in respect of apprenticeship training. This is a very real question, Mr. Chairman, and one to which I think we will have to turn our attention. Can we in 1962 expect the federal government, with its responsibility in matters of money and finance, with its responsibility in respect of external trade, with its responsibility for over-all financing of major national projects, to achieve the goal of full production and full employment, the raising of the standard of living, and at the same time be hampered in achieving that goal by the archaic legislation that exists in the province of Ontario?
Well, Mr. Chairman, I hope that the government will consider this question. I hope that the government will reassess the purpose for which this act was introduced, the purpose for which the legislation was passed and the purpose for which funds have been and are now being voted by parliament, and try to relate them to the great problem which exists in the country. I hope that before the question is put, the minister will reassure the committee that he will reassess the problem and that he will try to relate it to a greater extent than he has been able to demonstrate thus far to the funds being voted that are going to help rehabilitate and retrain those Canadian workers who, through no fault of their own, are unable to find gainful employment.

I believe that what the hon. member for Trinity has said should be given careful consideration by the government. I
Supply-Labour
feel this is the problem, that we are doing everything in the wrong order. We are putting the money in the wrong places in terms of priority. Certainly, we need vocational schools. However, let us find out where we need them and for what job we need them. Let us find out what people we should train. It is because of the planless, chaotic, confused state we have under this government today that we are doing the most fantastic things imaginable. This government is spending $124 million out of a vote of $188 million in Ontario, and yet Ontario may very well not even qualify for its share because they have not spent enough days in training unemployed people.
With over 200,000 people unemployed last winter in Ontario, that government did not train enough people to permit the Ontario government to qualify. The only provinces in fear of not qualifying were Ontario and Quebec. Yet, you have this distorted priority. The people were not trained but were on the welfare rolls and the governments are putting money into vocational schools which in many areas, I say from experience, are not going to be fully utilized for perhaps ten years.
They will be training people so there will be no unskilled unemployed in the future.

These schools are not even training people for the type of employment that will be available 10 or 20 years from now. Are we going to keep these unskilled unemployed for the next 20 years? Are they going to be the lost generation, the lost group of people, as a result of this government's policy? You can put it another way. Are these people going to remain unemployed and do nothing for the economy of this country for the next 20 years? I know people who have been unemployed for three years. The hon. member for Essex East said he has people who are coming to him every week end, and I expect other members have had the same experience. There has been no government directed program for retraining unemployed. There is an excellent editorial on this subject in the Toronto daily Star, and it reads in part:
Toronto's retraining program for the unemployed has hardly begun, though it was supposed to be well under way by midsummer. Why?
There is no lack of unemployed men and women -26,398 were asking the national employment service Toronto district office for jobs last week.
At the same time, there were 10,000 unfilled jobs in Toronto that these people could not take.

AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-22, to amend the Criminal Code (corporal punishment).
He said: Mr. Speaker, the origin of this bill, as most hon. members are probably aware by now, is the report of the joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons made in 1956 on capital punishment, corporal punishment and lotteries.
The recommendations of the committee include the following:
The committee kept two considerations in mind throughout its inquiry into corporal punishment as a part of the sentence of the court. The first was whether it deters those subjected to it from further crime and. second, whether it deters the public generally to a greater extent than other methods of punishment. The evidence did not justify the view that it will exercise any special reformative or deterrent influence on individuals upon whom it is administered and, on the whole, it appears to have the contrary effect. The committee concluded that the existence of corporal punishment affords no unique deterrence to crime. Accordingly, the committee recommends that corporal punishment be abolished for any of the offences for which it is presently prescribed in the Criminal Code.
The committee, representing members of all parties of this house and the other place, came to this conclusion after a most careful, thoughtful and thorough examination, after
[The Chairman.]
hearing testimony from many sectors of our country and summoning informed and expert witnesses on this subject.
The history of the movement to abolish corporal punishment here and in other countries is interesting because wherever it has been abolished, either within provincial jurisdiction-as it was recently in the province of Ontario-or within federal jurisdiction, as occurred in England, the abolition of this particular form of punishment has flown in the face of public opinion. In England approximately 75 per cent of the public disagreed with the action taken in abolishing corporal punishment.
I am confident that this is the situation in Canada today and has been for some years. I have seen no evidence-and I would be grateful if any hon. member who has encountered any evidence to the contrary would inform me of this-that this situation has changed materially since the report of the joint committee to which I referred a few moments ago.
I should like to refer to the experience in England. Last year I took the opportunity to place on the record excerpts from the report on corporal punishment handed down by the advisory council on the treatment of offenders. This advisory council was ordered by the home office in England. The report was presented to that parliament by the secretary of state for the home department by command of Her Majesty in November, 1960. The advisory council was formed as a result of increasing agitation within and without parliament in England concerning the increase in the incidence of crime in general and crimes of violence, in particular, and particularly strong pressure exerted from within the house of commons.
A substantial number of government members-that is, members of the Conservative party-in England had been making vociferous demands of the government to restore corporal punishment, which hon. members will recall had been abolished in that country some years before.
Last year I placed on the record the salient features of that report in connection with this measure. I would recommend the reading of the report to hon. members interested in this matter. In reviewing the salient features of the report last year I neglected to state that in the face of vociferous agitation within the Conservative party in the British house and abroad in the country the government accepted the report, flying in the face of approximately 75 per cent of public opinion to the contrary. Surely that was an act of courage on the part of that government and an example, in an enlightened way of not accepting public opinion. I neglected to include that salient fact in the summary of the British experience in

my speech on second reading of this bill last year. It is my opinion that the feeling in Canada today among those who are concerned with this matter is that we would be prepared to abolish corporal punishment for the adult groups, having acknowledged the futility of taking a hardened criminal, lashing him to a post and proceeding to apply the penalty in the quaint and crude manner prescribed under the Criminal Code.
I mentioned the province of Ontario a few moments ago. Again, it is significant that the province of Ontario under the leadership of George Wardrope, the then minister responsible for reform institutions in Ontario, should have abolished corporal punishment in that province. This was an act of political courage, I suggest, particularly when one recalls-and I am subject to correction here -that this action was taken a few months before a general election in that province. One could argue that the gentleman was elected in spite of that action rather than because of it, but it is significant to me that this action, an enlightened as well as a courageous one, should have met with a wide measure of support, certainly on the editorial pages of newspapers in Ontario.
I should like to turn the attention of the house today to the specific problem of the juvenile delinquent because, as I said a few moments ago, it is my opinion that the country is prepared to abolish corporal punishment for the adult group but that there is a reluctance not only among members of this house but among members of the public at large to abolish corporal punishment of the juvenile delinquent.
I should like to quote from the original report to this house concerning this question of the juvenile delinquent. I should also like to quote from the United Kingdom report, because this subject, as I shall point out later, is receiving increasing attention and is under study at this time by a committee set up by the Minister of Justice on January 8 of this year to inquire into the whole question of juvenile delinquency. It is my hope and expectation that following this inquiry we shall come to a final conclusion on this matter and satisfy ourselves that corporal punishment has no effective application in the field of the treatment of juvenile delinquents, and then proceed to abolish corporal punishment and place the name of Canada among those of the nations which have reached a degree of enlightenment enabling them to remove a barbaric and punitive form of punishment.
In the report of the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons, specific reference is made to the corporal punishment of young offenders. I quote:
Criminal Code
The committee gave special consideration to the problem of young offenders. Some of the arguments for extending the use of corporal punishment to young offenders as an effective deterrent against subsequent offences are reviewed in paragraph 13. The only suggestions made for increased use of corporal punishment were made by those who favoured its use for particular types of young offenders. The view was expressed that youths who had persisted, despite reasonable efforts at reform by probation and other methods, in offences against the person, property or public order, most commonly associated with street corner gangs, might be brought to their senses by the administration of corporal punishment. In this way, it was contended, they might be saved from a prison sentence which would probably lead to a confirmed criminal career.
Then the report continues:
The committee cannot accept these views. The evidence presented to the committee indicated that the special provisions formerly made in the United Kingdom for the caning or birching of young offenders were not effective and were gradually abandoned, in practice, in favour of probation and other methods of treatment which were found to be much more effective. The United Kingdom departmental committee on corporal punishment (1933) recommended abolition of caning young offenders. This recommendation was carried into effect in 1948, by which time caning had become virtually obsolete as a method of treatment or punishment.
Medical and psychiatric evidence presented to the committee suggested that little, if any, advantage would come from increased use of corporal punishment against young offenders. It was stated that such punishment would create an attitude of aggressive hostility in many cases which would militate against reform; and the experience of the juvenile and family court of Toronto with corporal punishment of juveniles supported this contention. The danger exists that any increased use of corporal punishment for young offenders might undermine and destroy the positive attempts made towards their reform and rehabilitation. It was also considered that the delay resulting from the necessity of allowing for a proper trial and appeal would destroy any good which an immediate application of corporal punishment might accomplish.
Finally, the report says:
The committee does not believe that any convincing case was made for extending the use of corporal punishment to young offenders.
I would remind hon. members that this question of the street corner gang and the kid in the leather jacket is not new. Suggestions have been made that this problem is increasing, but the factors which are involved and which were considered by the committee have, I submit, not changed in any material way since the date of this report.
Now I should like to refer to the report made in 1960 in the United Kingdom where special attention was paid to this question of corporal punishment for juvenile offences. I quote:
There seems to be a widespread feeling, based partly on these objections to the formalities of judicial corporal punishment and partly on those to the delay that must occur before the punishment is inflicted, that for young offenders the

Criminal Code
punishment should be either less formal or administered without waiting for the ordinary judicial processes. One suggestion put forward-
I might add, parenthetically, that this is a suggestion I have heard frequently from hon. members in private discussions on this subject.
-was that courts should have power to order young offenders to be caned by their parents, and another that the offenders should be handed over to their schools to be caned.
After mentioning that this particular point is discussed in another paragraph, the report goes on to say:
We do not see how either could be enforced. Another popular suggestion was that the police should be permitted to "cuff" or "spank" young offenders on the spot, or should take them to the police station to be caned immediately, and that they should be protected by law against the possible consequences of such actions.
Again, this is a popular opinion, a widely held view as to what might constitute a simple, quick and easy solution to this problem. Hon. members may recall several suggestions which have been put forward as to how these young punks can be treated. The report goes on:
Several of our older correspondents said that these practices were prevalent when they were young and that it was mainly because they themselves were dealt with summarily in such ways that they were better behaved in later life. We do not think, however, that such practices would now be found acceptable.
Then, discussing the reference which was made to the possibility of turning over young offenders to their parents for punishment, the report states in a later paragraph:
One suggestion that was put forward in relation to young offenders was that parents should be required to administer the penalty, if necessary under supervision, but this would clearly be impracticable, as well as objectionable in principle. A parent could not be required by law to chastise his child, nor could any sanction be imposed if he refused to do so.
Where the problem has come into sharp public focus, public opinion aroused and inquiry made into the question, we find once again that the thinking of experienced people in the field almost unanimously is that in England corporal punishment should not be restored and in Canada it should be abolished.
I mentioned earlier that the Minister of Justice has established a committee to implement a study of juvenile delinquency in Canada. I wish to read briefly from the terms of reference of the committee as contained in the press release of the Department of Justice dated January 8:
The committee will be charged with the responsibility of inquiring into and reporting upon the nature and extent of this problem in Canada and to make recommendations concerning steps which may be taken by the parliament and government

of Canada to meet the problem. It will hold discussions throughout Canada with appropriate authorities who work in, or are familiar with the field of juvenile delinquency and invite written briefs from interested private organizations and members of the public.
The director of the main committee will be Allen J. MacLeod, Q.C., commissioner of penitentiaries, a man who I am sure is known to many hon. members of this house. I am certain Mr. MacLeod would not object if I mention here that this fulfils a strong personal ambition of his. I am sure he has discussed this with many hon. members. He feels that this is one of the vital areas of study that must be inquired into in an effort to understand and solve the problems that occur in later life, and those he has to deal with in his capacity as commisioner of penitentiaries. Mr. MacLeod is a man of outstanding reputation, ability and character and will do an excellent job in this capacity. He is to be assisted by a supervisory committee to be composed of the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Justice whose sterling qualities I need not list because the reputation of the hon. member for Saint John-Albert speaks for itself, C. W. Harvison, commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and Mr. T. George Street, Q.C., chairman of the national parole board, who are outstanding in their respective fields.
I would hope that the committee of inquiry in its meetings with various groups across Canada would address itself particularly to the problem of corporal punishment for the juvenile offender.
A frequent argument one hears with respect to the retention of corporal punishment is that advanced by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe in the debate last year to the effect that we do not want to go soft, that we do not want to spare the rod and spoil the child. However, I have personally spoken to people who held this view and who, when serving as members of committees of inquiry into the question, when confronted with the cold facts of the testimony of experienced people in the field reluctantly found themselves unable to maintain the position they had adopted when first confronted with the problem. Records of committees of inquiry may be examined to substantiate what I have said.
I will conclude quickly by urging that the committee headed by Mr. MacLeod address itself to this question. I expect that the recommendation they will make on the subject will concur with that made by the interparliamentary committee in Canada and with that made by the more recent committee in England, and that in the reasonably near

future we can look forward to a time when corporal punishment will have been finally abolished in Canada.
